newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says millions of teen smokers face early death.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says millions of teen smokers face early death.

text.p: More than five million of today's American children face premature death from smoking-related diseases if current trends continue, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) predicted that of the 68.7 million children under 18 in the United States, 16.6 million would become smokers. The agency said its estimate was conservative and did not reflect an increase in teenage smoking that began in 1992.
"Over a third of high school students in America smoke, and it's going up," said Michael Eriksen, director of the CDC's Office on Smoking and Health. He said 82 percent of smokers started before 18.

"An adolescent decision made as an 11- or 12-year-old is going to result in a painful, premature and needless death for over five million of today's children," Eriksen said. "They will, on average, die 12 years early."
Smoking and related deaths could result in about $200 billion in future health care costs and approximately 64 million years of potential life lost, the CDC predicted.
Eriksen said the estimate of future deaths from smoking was based on census data, smoking patterns among young adults and current death rates from smoking.
In a separate study of state-by-state smoking rates, the CDC said 22.4 percent of adults nationwide were smokers in 1995, ranging from 13.2 percent in Utah to 27.8 in Kentucky.
Smoking decreased in some states while remaining fairly stable in others. The percentage of adults who smoke fell in California from 26 percent in 1984 to 15.5 percent in 1995.

The CDC said Utah was the only state that had achieved the national health objective for 2000 of reducing cigarette smoking among adults to less than 15 percent. Utah has many Mormons whose religious beliefs bar tobacco and alcohol use.

Increased cigarette taxess and a statewide media campaign caused cigarette consumption in Massachusetts to fall more than three times as fast as most other states, the CDC said. Per capita cigarette consumption fell 20 percent between 1992 and 1996 in Massachusetts, where taxes were raised from 26 to 51 cents per pack in 1992.

But Eriksen said "You need to do more than increase price" to reduce cigarette consumption. "You need to have a comprehensive programme that ideally and optimally increases price and uses a proportion of that revenue to fund tobacco education programmes and health education."
The CDC said the percentage of smokers who smoke every day ranged from 79.7 percent in New Jersey to 92.9 percent in Oklahoma.

The government says tobacco use among young people has increased dramatically in the past few years. Between 1991 and 1995 the percentage of eighth- and tenth-graders who smoked increased 34 percent. In 1995, more than a third of 12th-graders said they had smoked in the past month and daily smoking in that group was up to 21.6 percent.

The Food and Drug Administration has proposed stricter regulation of the sale and distribution of cigarettes to children, including banning free samples and most vending machines and requiring photo identification for anyone under 27 purchasing tobacco products.
